tagline: Ozark curves, forest overlooks and a lake built by the CCC
intro: Blue Buck Knob twists through Ozark hill country in Mark Twain National Forest, passing farmland, open pasture and densely wooded slopes. The Forest Service calls this a National Forest Scenic Byway and recommends an hour or two for its 24 miles. Its account emphasizes forest views from several stopping places, with shortleaf pine and mixed hardwoods among the trees.

Noblett Lake brings the drive into a Depression-era building project: the Civilian Conservation Corps constructed the lake while its workers lived at Camp Willow. Remnants of the camp can be seen on Forest Road 108, across Highway AP from the lake road. The 26-acre lake is now a recreation area with picnicking, fishing and canoeing.

From Cabool, the Forest Service’s route follows Highway 181 south to Highway AP and ends where AP meets Highway 14. Along the way are Indian Creek and Blue Buck overlooks, the Noblett recreation area and the Children’s Forest/Blue Hole Trailhead. That trailhead connects with the Ridge Runner and Ozark trails.

moments.title: Blue Buck Overlook
moments.text: Blue Buck Overlook is one of the named stopping places on the byway, with parking at Blue Buck Lookout. The Forest Service describes views of the forest from stops along this 24-mile drive. The surrounding road passes through a mixture of farmland, open pasture and wooded hillsides; shortleaf pine grows among mixed hardwoods.

moments.title: Noblett Lake
moments.text: The Civilian Conservation Corps built Noblett Lake during the Great Depression. The 26-acre lake impounds Noblett Creek just after the stream crosses Highway AP in Douglas County. Before reaching the lake, the creek flows southwest through numerous deeply cut meanders. At the recreation area, picnic tables and grills offer a stop beside water built by the CCC crew. The Forest Service describes picnic shade from sugar maples, shortleaf pines and black and white oaks.

moments.title: Camp Willow
moments.text: Camp Willow housed the Civilian Conservation Corps workers who constructed Noblett Lake during the Great Depression. The Forest Service identifies visible remnants of the camp about 2.5 miles east of Highway AP on Forest Road 108, opposite Noblett Lake Road. The lake and camp remnants connect the recreation site with the place that housed its builders.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service, Blue Buck Knob National Forest Scenic Byway
